source.title: Resource-Adaptive Successive Doubling for Hyperparameter Optimization with Large Datasets on High-Performance Computing Systems
source.authors: M. Aach; Rakesh Sarma; H. Neukirchen; Morris Riedel; Andreas Lintermann

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether increasing batch size during training can preserve or improve held-out performance, using a resource-adaptive schedule rather than the fixed large-batch comparisons in V5.
record.gate_note: Results comparing ASHA and RASDA bear on V5 because RASDA increases global batch size as training progresses and reports test-set metrics. Other HPO comparisons, cited prior findings, and the CFD and AM test results do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses batch-size scheduling to build an HPO scheduler and reports the performance of its selected models. It compares RASDA with ASHA, changing resource allocation, batch schedules and trial selection while searching architectural and optimizer hyperparameters. These results establish scheduler performance, not whether larger batches impair generalization or whether recipe changes remove an established batch-size penalty.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: RASDA reduces HPO runtime by up to approximately 1.9 times and generally maintains or improves selected-model quality. They attribute the quality preservation or improvement to progressive batch-size scaling. That attribution is not isolated experimentally, and the weak-scaling results include lower accuracy at 8 and 16 GPUs.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares a resource-adaptive scheduler that increases workers and global batch size during training with plain ASHA, which keeps training resources constant per trial. Learning-rate rescaling and warm-up are part of the reported setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The weak-scaling comparison reports reduced test accuracy at 8 GPUs and, to a lesser extent, 16 GPUs; accuracy is matched in almost all cases. The paper attributes the small-scale reduction to too few evaluated configurations and limited benefit from large-batch training.

fits_no_version.finding: RASDA-selected ImageNet models attain test accuracy 0.6766 versus ASHA's 0.6688 at 40 epochs, and 0.6340 versus 0.6250 in the 20-epoch scaling-factor ablation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Resource-adaptive HPO can select models with slightly higher held-out accuracy than ASHA within the tested training budgets.

fits_no_version.finding: In weak-scaling experiments, RASDA generally matches ASHA's selected-model accuracy but has lower accuracy at 8 and, less strongly, 16 GPUs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative solution quality of resource-adaptive HPO depends on the scale and number of configurations evaluated.

record.problems: The study evaluates scheduler comparisons, not a controlled fixed-batch-size sweep. The weak-scaling accuracy values are only plotted, and numerical uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise eligible results omitted. The CFD and AM test metrics are not rows for V5: the paper describes CFD test widths as extrapolation data and the AM test data as a different cylinder.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizer generalization under specified tuning budgets.

A large-batch penalty under fixed epoch budgets, its workload-dependent threshold, and its removal through recipe adaptation. No controlled comparison isolates these effects from HPO selection and other hyperparameter differences.
The relationship between magnitude-aware sharpness and generalization gaps.
Accuracy changes after removing memorized rather than random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Correct numerical extraction does not make the scheduler comparisons tests of V5. The statements about large-batch generalization in Sections 2.4 and 3.2 rely on prior literature; no new controlled batch-size experiment is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization are not tested.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Optimizer generalization is not compared as a claim; optimizer type is a search hyperparameter.
No language model results. The study compares adaptive batch-size scheduling with ASHA, not a controlled sweep over fixed batch sizes; weak-scaling accuracy results are figure-based.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Trained using plain ASHA with a constant number of GPUs and global batch size.
rows.note: Reference condition for the RASDA comparison.
rows.check: The value 0.6688 is correct, but it describes the best trial selected by ASHA, averaged over three seeds. It is an HPO-method comparator, not a measurement of V5.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Trained using RASDA, progressively increasing GPU allocation and global batch size.

conditions.value: global batch size increases from 256 to 2,048; GPUs per trial increase from 2 to 16

rows.note: RASDA's test accuracy is higher than ASHA's in this comparison.
rows.check: The value 0.6766 and reported batch schedule are correct. The improvement over 0.6688 compares HPO-selected models under different schedulers; it does not establish that batch-size adaptation removes a large-batch penalty. This should not be a V5 result row.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Trained using plain ASHA with a constant number of GPUs and global batch size.
rows.note: Reference condition in the reduction/scaling-factor ablation.
rows.check: The value 0.6250 is correct, but it is the ASHA-selected model's accuracy in a scheduler ablation, not an independent batch-size comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Trained using RASDA with scaling and reduction factors set to 4.
rows.note: RASDA accuracy exceeds ASHA in this ablation.
rows.check: The value 0.6340 is correct. Changing both reduction and scaling factors changes trial elimination and resource allocation; the selected-model improvement over ASHA does not measure V5.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Trained using ASHA in the weak-scaling comparison.
rows.note: Text says RASDA has reduced test accuracy only at 8 GPUs and, to a lesser extent, 16 GPUs; the plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Figure 3 reports HPO-method performance while the number of evaluated configurations increases with total GPU count. Total GPUs are not a controlled per-model batch-size treatment. This should not be a V5 comparator row.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Trained using RASDA in the weak-scaling comparison.
rows.baseline: ASHA; accuracy matched in almost all cases
rows.note: The text reports lower accuracy at 8 GPUs and, to a lesser extent, 16 GPUs; the plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: The text confirms lower RASDA accuracy at 8 and, less strongly, 16 GPUs, with matching accuracy in almost all other cases. These are scheduler outcomes confounded by configuration count and selection, so they do not establish a partial V5 effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
